items.question: An Indian pharmaceutical company is designing a three-tier classification that routes AI use cases to light-touch, standard or full governance review. A working group has proposed candidate criteria for placing a use case into a tier. Which TWO criteria should determine the tier? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The severity and reversibility of the consequence if the output is wrong — a patient-facing or regulatory-submission error against an internal drafting error.
options.B: The model tier selected, on the basis that higher-capability models can perform a wider range of tasks and therefore carry more inherent risk into any deployment.
options.C: Whether the output is acted on without a competent human reviewing it first, since that determines whether an error reaches the world unfiltered.
options.D: The projected monthly token spend for the use case, which is the figure most consistently available and comparable across the proposals the group receives.
options.E: Whether the capability was built in-house or purchased, since purchased products have already passed through the supplying vendor's own assurance process.

items.question: An AI policy exception is granted because a required control cannot be implemented before a committed launch date. What is the purpose of the compensating control recorded alongside the exception?

options.A: To document the reasons the required control could not be implemented within the timescale that was available.
options.B: To transfer accountability for the exception from the approving body to the team that requested it.
options.C: To demonstrate to an auditor that the exception process was followed even though the outcome is non-compliant.
options.D: To bring the residual risk down to a level the approver is willing to carry for the life of the exception.

items.question: A Portuguese hospital group's discharge-summary assistant has a system card approved fourteen months ago. The card names the model in use, lists the data sources the assistant retrieves from, records evaluation results on the group's own discharge cases, and describes the clinician sign-off step. The group's standard requires the card to be re-issued whenever a change makes something the card asserts no longer true. Which TWO of the following require re-issue? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Extending the retrieval corpus to include nursing notes, which were not previously reachable by the assistant.
options.B: Rerunning the evaluation suite against the unchanged configuration as part of the group's quarterly assurance cycle, with results inside the previously recorded range.
options.C: Upgrading to a newer model tier, with the evaluation suite rerun afterwards and the scores improving on every measure.
options.D: Correcting a formatting defect in the output template so that section headings render properly in the electronic patient record.
options.E: Confirming at the annual review that the clinician sign-off step is unchanged and continues to operate exactly as the card describes.

items.question: A Korean online brokerage's Claude-based research summariser omitted a material risk disclosure from company summaries for eleven days; roughly 9,000 retail clients viewed an affected summary. The firm's internal standard states that any event which may have influenced a client investment decision is escalated to the disclosure committee within 24 hours of confirmation. The failure was confirmed this morning. The head of engineering notes that no client has complained and no affected trade has been identified, and proposes escalating once the impact analysis is finished next week. What is the correct course?

options.A: Complete the impact analysis first, so that the committee receives a quantified view of how many clients were affected rather than being asked to decide on visibly incomplete information.
options.B: Escalate only if a client complains or an affected trade is identified, since the standard is concerned with actual detriment rather than theoretical exposure.
options.C: Disclose directly to affected clients and to the regulator immediately, bypassing the committee, because any delay compounds the original failure.
options.D: Escalate to the disclosure committee now: the trigger is possible influence on a client decision and that is already confirmed, with the analysis supplied to the committee as it develops.

items.question: Why should the function that reviews and challenges AI risk assessments report through a line separate from the function that builds and runs AI systems?

options.A: So that reviewers have the technical depth required to evaluate model and architecture choices on their own terms.
options.B: So that the cost of the review function can be carried centrally rather than charged against individual project budgets.
options.C: So that a challenge to a delivery decision cannot be overruled by the person whose delivery timeline the challenge affects.
options.D: So that regulators and auditors have a single named contact point for questions about the organisation's AI estate.

items.question: An Emirati port operator retired a Claude-based berth-planning pilot nine months ago and marked its register entry 'retired'. A scheduled reconciliation has now found the pilot's gateway credential still active, carrying low but non-zero traffic originating from a scheduled job inside a business unit's automation account. The team that sponsored the pilot was disbanded at the same time it was retired. Which conclusion is best supported, and should drive the remediation?

options.A: Decommissioning is recorded as a register status change with no corresponding technical action, so 'retired' in the register carries no assurance that a system has actually stopped.
options.B: The reconciliation cadence is too slow; had reconciliation run monthly instead of on the current cycle, the live credential would have been detected far earlier.
options.C: Business unit automation accounts should not be permitted to hold gateway credentials at all, and this account should be removed from the gateway's issuing scope with its workloads moved to platform-managed identities.
options.D: The register lacks a field for recording a system's technical dependencies, which is why the scheduled job was never identified when the pilot was retired.

items.question: An Austrian retailer licenses a recruitment platform that it assessed and approved three years ago. The vendor has just announced a candidate-summarisation feature, enabled by default for all tenants at the next release, with no change to the contract or the commercial terms. The retailer's AI policy requires any AI system processing personnel data to be registered and assessed before use. The HR director's position is that nothing has been procured, so there is nothing to register. Which analysis is correct?

options.A: The policy applies: a new AI capability will process personnel data on the retailer's behalf, so it requires registration and assessment regardless of whether a separate purchase took place.
options.B: The policy does not apply, because the feature ships inside a product already assessed and approved; re-assessing on every vendor feature release would make the policy unworkable at scale.
options.C: The policy applies only once HR actually uses the feature, since no personnel data is processed until someone asks for a candidate summary to be generated.
options.D: The policy is the wrong instrument here; this is a change-management matter for the platform's service owner and should follow the retailer's standard vendor release process.

items.question: Outside the normal periodic review cycle, which event should trigger a re-assessment of a third-party AI product already in use?

options.A: The vendor publishes an updated independent security attestation covering the same scope as the previous one.
options.B: The vendor redesigns the product's user interface and navigation, so the organisation must reissue its user guidance and retrain staff.
options.C: The vendor changes the model or the model provider behind the product, or extends what the product does with customer data.
options.D: The organisation's usage grows past the volume band assumed in the vendor's original commercial proposal.

items.question: A Danish employment agency's Claude-based screening assistant applied an outdated eligibility rule for six weeks, causing about 300 applicants to be told they did not qualify for a training scheme they in fact qualified for. The incident is contained and the rule is corrected. The incident lead is preparing the notification decision. Which TWO points should govern how that decision is made? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The decision belongs to a named accountable executive advised by legal and communications, not to the incident lead or the engineering team who found the fault.
options.B: Notification should wait until the agency can confirm precisely which of the 300 applicants would have qualified, so that nobody is contacted unnecessarily.
options.C: The affected individuals need a remedy alongside the notice — a reopened application or a re-decision — because a notice without a route to correction transfers the burden onto them.
options.D: Because the error originated in a rule configuration rather than in the model's output, the agency should treat it as an ordinary process defect and use its standard service-correction letter.
options.E: Notification should be limited to applicants who have already contacted the agency to dispute their result, since the rest have shown no interest in the outcome.

items.question: A Belgian rail operator's AI approval board consists of the CTO, the head of data, an enterprise architect and a procurement lead. It has approved thirty-one use cases in eighteen months. An external review examined the four cases where harm later materialised — all of them customer-facing decisions about compensation for delayed journeys — and found that the board minutes for those four contain detailed discussion of data flows, model choice and supplier terms, but no discussion at all of what happens to a passenger when the system gets it wrong. What change to the board addresses the root cause?

options.A: Require the requesting team to submit a written risk assessment ahead of each meeting so the board reviews prepared analysis rather than reacting to a presentation given on the day.
options.B: Appoint an external adviser with AI ethics expertise as a standing member to provide independent challenge on the societal impact of the proposals the internal members are close to.
options.C: Rotate board membership on an annual cycle so that a wider range of functional perspectives is brought to bear on approval decisions over time.
options.D: Add the accountable owner of the affected business process — passenger services — as a standing member with a decision right, so the consequence has an owner in the room.

items.question: A Czech engineering consultancy's egress logs show that a project team has spent eight months sending structural calculation notes to a consumer AI product from personal accounts on company laptops. The notes contain a client's unpublished design drawings held under a non-disclosure agreement. Access to the service was blocked at the proxy this morning as soon as the logs were reviewed, and the team has been told to stop. The AI governance lead has just been handed the evidence. What is the next step?

options.A: Report the confidentiality exposure to the client straight away, since the non-disclosure agreement has been breached and delay worsens the consultancy's position.
options.B: Establish the scope — what data left, over what period, to which service, and under which account terms — before any notification or enforcement decision is taken.
options.C: Extend the proxy block to every consumer AI service and revoke local administrator rights across the consultancy, so that no comparable route remains open to anyone.
options.D: Register the use in the AI inventory and put it through the standard assessment so that it becomes a governed use case on the sanctioned platform.

items.question: A team argues that because a wrong output was generated by the model rather than by any person, the organisation is not answerable for the resulting harm. What is the correct principle?

options.A: The organisation deployed the system and acted on its output, so the outcome is the organisation's whichever component produced it.
options.B: Accountability is shared with the model provider in proportion to the provider's contribution to the error, as established by the incident investigation.
options.C: The organisation is answerable only where it can be shown to have departed from the provider's documented guidance for using the model.
options.D: Accountability rests with the individual who authored the prompt, since that is the instruction that shaped the output in question.

items.question: A Swedish architecture practice issues its AI acceptable-use policy through the employee handbook, acknowledged at onboarding. About a third of production work on a large hospital project is delivered by freelance draughtspeople engaged through an agency, working on their own laptops with access to the practice's cloud file share. A reviewer finds AI-generated specification text in a deliverable produced by one of them, describing a fire-rating standard that does not exist. What is the governing weakness?

options.A: The practice has no reliable way to detect AI-generated text, so it should apply a detection tool to every incoming deliverable before it is accepted into the project record.
options.B: The freelancers work on their own laptops and are outside endpoint monitoring, so the practice should require practice-issued devices for all contract staff before granting file share access.
options.C: The policy is bound to the employment relationship and does not reach the people producing a third of the work; the obligation has to sit in the engagement contract and the agency's terms.
options.D: The specification text should have been caught in the practice's design review, so the remedy is to add an AI-content question to the existing review checklist and brief reviewers on it.

items.question: A Vietnamese digital bank is extending its incident severity matrix to cover AI failures. The current matrix rates severity on number of users affected and duration of the outage. Applied to recent events, it rated an AI failure that produced incorrect but entirely plausible tax statements for twelve customers at the lowest severity, while a forty-minute degradation of an internal dashboard rated two levels higher. Which set of dimensions should the AI severity rating be built on?

options.A: Number of affected users, outage duration and the model tier in use, so that AI severity stays comparable with the existing matrix and can be applied by the same triage team without retraining.
options.B: Whether the output reached a person or drove an action, how severe and reversible the consequence is, and whether an oversight step should have caught it.
options.C: Financial exposure estimated at the moment of declaration, so that AI incidents can be prioritised against the bank's other operational risk events on a single monetary scale.
options.D: Confidence scores logged by the system when the failure occurred, so that severity reflects how far the model's behaviour departed from its expected operating range at the time.

items.question: In a RACI covering approval of a new AI use case, what distinguishes a Consulted party from an Informed one?

options.A: A Consulted party can veto the decision outright; an Informed party can only have an objection recorded in the minutes.
options.B: A Consulted party attends the approval meeting in person; an Informed party receives the papers in advance and may submit comments.
options.C: A Consulted party is drawn from the second line of defence, while an Informed party is drawn from the first line.
options.D: A Consulted party's input must be sought and addressed before the decision is taken; an Informed party is told once it has been.

items.question: A Scottish renewables developer ran a shadow AI sweep across corporate card spend, expense claims and vendor invoices, and found nothing beyond the two registered platforms. A subsequent code review turned up model API calls in three internal repositories, authenticated with keys that do not map to any corporate billing account. Two of the three run in production against turbine maintenance records. Which TWO detection methods would have found this use? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Scanning source repositories and CI configuration for model provider SDK imports, API endpoint hostnames and credential patterns.
options.B: Reviewing corporate card statements and vendor invoices again at a lower value threshold than the sweep used, to catch small or trial-tier charges.
options.C: Inspecting egress from build agents and production workloads for outbound connections to model provider API hostnames.
options.D: Requiring engineering managers to attest each quarter that none of their teams calls an unapproved model API from any repository they own.
options.E: Auditing single sign-on application consents to identify AI products that have been connected to the corporate identity tenant.

items.question: A Peruvian mining company's AI board approved a geotechnical-risk summarisation assistant subject to three conditions: an evaluation set covering five years of incident reports, a documented escalation route to a qualified geotechnical engineer, and a post-implementation review at six months. The assistant went live nine months ago. None of the three conditions has been evidenced, no record shows anyone tracking them, and the approval register displays the status 'Approved'. What does this indicate, and what should be fixed?

options.A: Conditional approval is being recorded as unconditional: conditions need owners, dates and a closure gate, and the status should read as approved with open conditions until each is evidenced.
options.B: The board attached too many conditions to a single decision and should instead defer approval entirely until the requesting team has already satisfied every condition it intends to impose.
options.C: The missing control is the post-implementation review; had it been scheduled at the point of approval, it would have surfaced the two outstanding conditions within the intended six months.
options.D: The three conditions were operational rather than governance matters, and should have been raised as delivery requirements with the project manager rather than attached to a board approval.

items.question: AI incident postmortems are conducted blamelessly — describing what people did and why it made sense to them at the time, without attributing fault. What does that convention buy the organisation?

options.A: It keeps the postmortem document suitable for sharing with external auditors and reviewers without further redaction.
options.B: It guarantees that no individual faces any consequence for an error, which is what makes staff willing to take part at all.
options.C: It produces a fuller and more accurate account, by removing the incentive to leave detail out.
options.D: It shortens the time needed to produce the postmortem, by avoiding arguments about who was responsible for what.

items.question: A Greek shipping line's Claude-based cargo documentation assistant produced incorrect dangerous-goods classifications on shipping documents for two days. The incident was declared thirty minutes ago and the assistant is disabled. Operations, compliance and IT are each contacting customers, port agents and the classification society separately, and two of them have already given different figures for how many shipments are affected. Port agents need corrected classifications before the next vessel sails at 18:00. What should the incident lead do next?

options.A: Ask all three teams to pause outbound communication until the affected shipment count is confirmed, then issue a single agreed statement to every audience at once.
options.B: Establish a single source of truth for incident facts and a named communications owner, and require every outbound message to be drawn from it.
options.C: Escalate to the executive sponsor so that a decision can be taken on whether the classification society must be notified formally.
options.D: Move compliance and IT onto the technical investigation and leave operations to handle all external communication on its own.

items.question: A Malaysian telco's care team is building a Claude assistant and wants to use ten years of contact-centre transcripts as few-shot examples and as its evaluation set. The transcripts sit in a system owned by the customer operations directorate; the AI team obtained a copy informally from a data-engineering colleague. The telco's governance standard requires that reuse of a data set for a purpose other than the one it was collected for be authorised by that data set's owner. The AI team's position is that the data never leaves the company. What is the governance defect?

options.A: The transcripts contain customer identifiers and ought to be de-identified before any use in prompts or evaluation, and the absence of that step is the defect the standard exists to catch.
options.B: Few-shot examples and evaluation cases must be drawn from disjoint samples, and using the same ten-year corpus for both will contaminate the evaluation and overstate measured quality.
options.C: Ten years of transcripts far exceeds what the use case needs, and the team should have requested a smaller and more recent sample proportionate to the task it is supporting.
options.D: The data is being used for a purpose other than the one it was collected for, and only the owner can authorise that change; the informal transfer bypassed the decision entirely.

items.question: What makes a board-level AI risk appetite statement operable rather than decorative?

options.A: It states limits an approval body can apply to a specific proposal — which categories of decision may be automated, and what must always retain human sign-off.
options.B: It is reviewed and reaffirmed by the board annually, with the review recorded in the minutes and reported onward to the audit committee for assurance.
options.C: It is expressed in the same language and on the same scale as the organisation's other risk appetite statements, so that AI risk can be aggregated with them.
options.D: It is communicated to every member of staff through the AI usage policy, so that everyone understands the level of risk the organisation is prepared to accept.

items.question: An organisation reports 'percentage of staff who completed AI policy training' as its primary AI governance metric. Why is that a weak choice?

options.A: It is a lagging indicator, and governance metrics should be leading indicators that predict where the next control failure will occur.
options.B: It measures an input the organisation controls completely, and will read close to full compliance whether or not any prohibited use has actually stopped.
options.C: It cannot be benchmarked against comparable organisations, so the board is given a figure with no external reference against which to judge whether it is good or bad.
options.D: It excludes contractors and agency staff, and until they are brought into scope the figure cannot properly be reported to the board at all.

items.question: A Turkish conglomerate has acquired a 200-person insurtech. Due diligence covered financials, intellectual property and security, but not AI. On the first day of integration the acquirer finds four customer-facing AI features in production, none of them registered anywhere, one of which generates pricing recommendations that underwriters accept without change in most cases. The group standard requires all AI in the group to be registered and risk-tiered within ninety days of acquisition. Which TWO actions should be prioritised inside that window? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Register all four as use cases with a named accountable owner drawn from the group's structure, and tier them on consequence and autonomy.
options.B: Migrate all four features onto the acquirer's model gateway before the ninety days expire, so that they fall under central logging and credential control immediately.
options.C: Establish what the target's customer contracts and its own AI vendor contracts say about model data use, since those terms transferred with the business and now bind the group.
options.D: Suspend the pricing-recommendation feature until the acquirer's approval board has reviewed it, on the grounds that it affects customers and has never been assessed.
options.E: Require every engineer at the target to complete the group's AI policy training and sign the acceptable-use attestation within the first month of integration.

items.question: An analyst at an Italian energy retailer believes the Claude-based retention-offer assistant is systematically offering worse terms to customers in certain postcodes. She raised it with her line manager, who replied that the model receives no postcode input and closed the conversation. Six weeks later nothing has been logged anywhere, and the assistant continues to run. What does the governance framework most need here?

options.A: Commission an evaluation of the assistant's outputs segmented by postcode, so the analyst's claim can be tested against data rather than argued from what inputs the model receives.
options.B: Introduce a rule that any concern about model fairness is escalated to the second line of defence for determination rather than being resolved by the employee's own line manager.
options.C: A route by which any employee can log an AI concern directly into the governance record, where it is triaged and closed with a recorded outcome, whatever their manager's view.
options.D: Make bias testing mandatory at approval time for every customer-facing AI system, so that concerns of this kind are identified and dealt with before the system reaches production.

items.question: A Colombian retail group has an approved Claude-based complaint triage assistant running in its home market. It now wants to run the identical system — same code, same prompts, same model, same hosting — for a recently acquired Ecuadorian subsidiary. The group standard requires re-approval wherever the risk profile changes materially. Which TWO things must be assessed before the extension proceeds? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Whether the evaluation set represents the subsidiary's complaint mix, product range and language use, since the recorded performance was measured entirely on home-market cases.
options.B: Whether the underlying model performs equivalently at the higher request volume, since combined traffic across both markets will roughly double.
options.C: Who the accountable owner is in the subsidiary, and whether the escalation route to a human complaint handler exists and is staffed there.
options.D: Whether the subsidiary's staff have completed the group's AI policy training, which the group treats as a precondition for operating any system in a group entity.
options.E: Whether the system should be rebuilt on the subsidiary's own infrastructure so that the two markets do not share a technical dependency.

items.question: Why should an AI usage policy state what is permitted rather than only listing what is prohibited?

options.A: A permitted-use statement gives staff a decidable answer for the cases the prohibition list does not name, which is most of them.
options.B: Prohibition lists cannot be enforced without a disciplinary framework, whereas a permitted-use statement enforces itself through the sanctioned platform.
options.C: A permitted-use statement removes the need to maintain a list of named tools, because permissions can be written against categories of use instead.
options.D: Prohibition lists must be reviewed far more frequently than permission lists, because new AI products appear continuously and each one requires assessment.

items.question: A Japanese consumer electronics maker routes all Claude access through an internal gateway; each registered use case receives its own credential with a declared purpose recorded against it. A platform engineer reviewing gateway logs notices that the credential registered for supplier contract summarisation is also carrying prompts that classify the tone of employee performance review text. The team says it is a small experiment and that no decisions are being taken from the output. What is the correct response?

options.A: Treat the deviation as minor, record it in the log review notes, and ask the team to register the second use case when the next quarterly registration cycle opens.
options.B: Revoke the credential immediately, accepting that this also halts the approved contract-summarisation work until the team completes a fresh registration covering both uses.
options.C: Add employee performance content to the gateway's blocked patterns so that these prompts are rejected whichever credential submits them, without acting against the team.
options.D: Stop the unapproved use now and require it to be registered and assessed as its own use case with its own credential, since the declared purpose is the unit of approval.

items.question: A Philippine business process outsourcer runs a monthly AI risk forum whose terms of reference say it 'reviews and notes AI risks and escalates as appropriate'. Over the past year it noted forty risks; thirty-one remain open, and none was ever escalated, because 'as appropriate' was never defined and no member holds authority to halt or vary a client programme. What change would make the forum effective?

options.A: Appoint the chief risk officer as chair, so that the forum is led by someone senior enough for its views to carry weight with the client programme directors who would have to act on them.
options.B: Give the forum defined decision rights and a written escalation trigger — what it can require, what it must refer upward, and by when — so that noting a risk produces an owned, dated action.
options.C: Narrow the forum's scope to the highest-tier client programmes, so that the thirty-one open items reduce to a list the forum can realistically work through each month.
options.D: Move the forum to a fortnightly cadence so that open risks are revisited far more often and none can sit untouched for a full year before being discussed again.

items.question: Following press coverage of an AI failure at a competitor, an Argentine bank's board has asked the CEO to report at next month's meeting on which customer-facing decisions are made or influenced by an AI system, and who signs off each one. The bank's AI register holds system name, business unit, model and go-live date. It does not record whether a system is customer-facing, whether its output is acted on without human review, or who the accountable owner is. What should the chief risk officer do next?

options.A: Commission a full re-registration of the entire estate against a revised schema, and inform the board at next month's meeting that a complete answer will follow once that exercise has finished.
options.B: Answer from the register as it stands, flag clearly that the three fields the board asked about are not held today, and propose a schema change for the next registration cycle.
options.C: Run a targeted exercise against the specific question — for each registered system, whether it touches a customer decision, whether output is acted on unreviewed, and who owns it — and make those permanent register fields.
options.D: Commission an independent external review of the AI estate so that the board receives an assurance opinion from a third party rather than management's own account of the bank's exposure to the risk raised.

items.question: An internal standard requires a system card to be signed before an AI system is released to production. Who should sign it?

options.A: The accountable owner of the use case, since the card is a set of assertions somebody has to stand behind.
options.B: The engineering lead who built the system, as the person with the most detailed knowledge of how it actually behaves.
options.C: The chair of the AI governance board, as the representative of the body that approved the deployment into production.
options.D: The organisation's data protection officer, as the reviewer of the data classes the system processes and retains.

items.question: A Nigerian retail bank has nine registered AI use cases, all running on a single model provider through one gateway; two of them support regulated customer communications and two are used inside the branch network's daily operating process. The board's operational resilience standard requires the bank to identify and plan for the loss of any single critical supplier. The head of architecture proposes maintaining a second provider in parallel for all nine. Which TWO points should shape the response? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Concentration should be managed per use case against its criticality, so that only the uses the bank genuinely cannot operate without justify the cost of a maintained alternative.
options.B: Running a second provider in parallel across all nine removes the concentration exposure, because either provider can serve any request at any moment.
options.C: Each critical use case needs a rehearsed fallback that does not depend on the provider — including a documented manual or degraded process — since a second model needs its own prompts and evaluation before it can be trusted.
options.D: Concentration is addressed through the contract's availability commitments, so the right response is to negotiate stronger service levels rather than to change the architecture.
options.E: The gateway rather than the provider is the real single point of failure, so applications should be permitted to call the provider directly as a bypass route when the gateway is unavailable.

items.question: A Romanian telecommunications operator's Claude-based network operations agent executes remediation runbooks autonomously when its confidence threshold is met. One runbook reroutes traffic away from a regional core node; reversing it takes about forty minutes and the reroute itself briefly degrades service for roughly 90,000 subscribers. The change advisory board wants a control on this specific runbook without removing the agent's autonomy elsewhere. Which control fits?

options.A: Raise the confidence threshold at which the agent will run that runbook so it executes only when highly confident, and log every invocation for review at the weekly operations meeting.
options.B: Require the agent to write its reasoning to the operations log immediately before executing, so an operator reading the log afterwards can identify a wrong decision quickly and begin the reversal.
options.C: Restrict the runbook to off-peak hours, when the number of subscribers affected by a mistaken reroute would be substantially lower than during the daytime peak.
options.D: Require a named on-shift network engineer to authorise this action before it executes, with the agent's reasoning and the affected node shown at the point of decision.

items.question: A Hungarian pharmaceutical distributor's IT team discovers that 140 staff have installed browser extensions that summarise or rewrite the current page, several of which request permission to read and change data on all sites. The extensions are free, so nothing appears in spend data, and they authenticate to their own vendors rather than to the corporate identity tenant, so nothing appears in application consent logs. Which TWO controls address this class of use? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Move extension installation to an allow-list managed through enterprise browser policy, so that only reviewed extensions can be installed on managed devices.
options.B: Add the vendors' domains to the egress block list, which stops the current extensions working until staff find replacements that are not yet listed.
options.C: Inventory the extensions installed across the managed fleet and assess them against the permissions they request, treating broad read-and-change host permissions as the risk driver.
options.D: Require staff to declare any browser extension they use in the annual AI self-declaration, so that extension use is reflected in the register alongside other tools.
options.E: Raise the frequency of the AI policy reminder email to monthly and name browser extensions explicitly as a prohibited category of tool.

items.question: An assurance team is testing whether an AI governance control operates as designed. What distinguishes evidence from attestation?

options.A: Attestation is given by the control owner, whereas evidence must be produced by a party independent of the first line of defence.
options.B: Attestation is a statement that the control operated; evidence is an artefact the control itself produced, which the tester can inspect directly.
options.C: Attestation covers a whole period, whereas evidence captures a point in time and must be sampled across the period before it means anything.
options.D: Attestation is acceptable for lower-tier controls, whereas evidence is required only for the controls that the annual assurance plan designates as key and tests in depth.

items.question: Nine months ago a Taiwanese semiconductor equipment maker's Claude-based service-report generator produced part numbers that did not exist, and field engineers ordered against them. The postmortem action — add a validation step that checks generated part numbers against the parts master — was implemented, tested and closed. The same failure has now recurred: the validation runs on the report's structured parts field, but the assistant also emits part numbers inside the free-text recommendations section, which is not validated. What should the second postmortem conclude about the governance process rather than about the defect?

options.A: The original action was implemented exactly as written, so this is a new defect rather than a recurrence and should be handled as a fresh incident with its own action.
options.B: The validation should move from the structured field to a check applied across the whole generated document, which would have caught both the original failure and this one.
options.C: Closure was verified against implementation rather than against whether the failure mode could still occur, so closure criteria have to test the failure mode, not the task.
options.D: Nine months is too long for a postmortem action to remain relevant, so actions should carry a review date at which their continued sufficiency is reconfirmed.

items.question: A Bulgarian online travel agency uses a supplied customer messaging platform whose AI reply-suggestion feature gave travellers incorrect refund-eligibility statements for three days. The agency learned of it from the vendor's public status page, four days after the vendor's own internal detection, and had to answer its customers with no account of what had happened. The contract covers security, availability and support; nothing addresses notification of AI behaviour failures. What should the agency require going forward?

options.A: A clause requiring the vendor to remediate any defect in the AI feature within a defined period, backed by service credits if that deadline is missed.
options.B: A right for the agency's internal audit function to audit the vendor's AI development, testing and release process annually, with findings shared between both parties.
options.C: A commitment that the vendor will not change the model behind the reply-suggestion feature without the agency's prior written consent on each occasion.
options.D: A notification clause with defined triggers, a maximum time from the vendor's own detection to notifying the agency, and a minimum content set for the notice.

items.question: An executive instructs a team to deploy an AI use case without the required governance review, saying they accept the risk personally. What makes that a legitimate risk acceptance rather than a bypass?

options.A: It is recorded as an exception describing the risk, with an expiry, and signed by the executive within their delegated authority.
options.B: It is reported to the governance board at its next meeting so that the board is aware the deployment has already taken place.
options.C: It is supported by a written statement from the team confirming that they raised the governance requirement before proceeding.
options.D: It is limited to a pilot population, keeping the exposure small enough for a single executive to carry personally.

items.question: A Thai consumer lender's marketing site states that its Claude-based eligibility assistant 'checks your application against every one of our lending criteria before you submit'. The approved system card records that the assistant checks six of the eleven criteria and flags the remaining five for the applicant to confirm manually. The head of governance found the discrepancy while reviewing the site for an unrelated reason. Applications are running at about 3,000 a week. What should the head of governance do next?

options.A: Ask marketing to soften the wording at the next scheduled site update and record the discrepancy in the governance log for the quarterly report.
options.B: Have the claim corrected or removed now, and raise an incident so that the population who applied while it was live can be scoped.
options.C: Extend the assistant to check all eleven criteria so the published claim becomes accurate, and set a delivery date with the engineering team.
options.D: Refer the wording to legal for an opinion on whether it amounts to a misleading statement before any action is taken on the site.

items.question: A Ghanaian mobile money operator's Claude-based fraud triage assistant wrongly froze about 5,000 customer wallets for fourteen hours. The chief risk officer is writing a two-page note for the board, which meets in three days while the investigation is still open. Which THREE items must the note contain? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: What happened in plain terms, how many customers were affected, and what those customers actually experienced during the fourteen hours.
options.B: The prompt and model configuration in force at the time, so that the board can form its own view on whether the technical design was appropriate.
options.C: Whether the control environment failed as designed or was simply absent, and which specific control is being changed as a result.
options.D: What remains unknown at the time of writing, and the date by which the board will be told.
options.E: A comparison of the operator's AI incident rate against other mobile money providers, so the board can judge its relative performance.

items.question: A Sri Lankan apparel manufacturer's HR team has begun using a Claude assistant to score internal promotion applications against the company's competency framework. The scores are printed in the promotion panel's pack, and the panel says it treats them as one input among several. The company's AI policy requires customer-affecting AI to be registered, tiered and given a named owner, and is silent on employee-affecting AI. What is the correct governance position?

options.A: The policy is silent on employee-affecting AI, so registration is not required; the HR team should record the assistant in its own procedure manual and in the promotion panel's terms of reference.
options.B: The scores should be removed from the panel pack altogether, because a panel that has seen a numeric score cannot genuinely treat it as one input among several.
options.C: The practice is acceptable provided the panel records its reasons whenever it departs from a score, which evidences that independent judgement was exercised in each case.
options.D: Employee-affecting decisions carry the same accountability requirements as customer-affecting ones; the policy's scope is the defect, and this use must be registered, tiered and owned.

items.question: A responsible scaling approach grants an AI system permissions in graduated steps — suggest, then act with confirmation, then act autonomously — rather than all at once. What does each step need in order to function as a gate?

options.A: A longer observation period than the step before it, so that rarer failure modes have time to appear under production conditions.
options.B: A separate approval from the governance board, so that no single team can advance a system through the ladder unchallenged.
options.C: A pre-agreed measure of whether the previous step performed acceptably, and a stated threshold that has to be met before advancing.
options.D: A distinct system card version, so that the deployed configuration at each level of autonomy is separately documented and signed.

items.question: A French luxury goods group's executive committee has exempted a flagship AI-first customer experience programme, covering seven customer-facing use cases, from the group's AI approval process for twelve months 'so the programme can move at pace', directing the governance team to review the outputs retrospectively at the end. The group risk framework permits the executive committee to accept risk within its delegated authority provided acceptances are recorded. The head of AI governance must respond. What is the strongest response?

options.A: Convert the decision into a recorded exception: named accepting executive, scope limited to the seven use cases, compensating controls, a shorter expiry, and defined stop conditions.
options.B: Decline to operate the exemption on the grounds that the approval process is mandated by the group risk framework, and escalate the matter to the board's risk committee.
options.C: Continue reviewing the programme informally and without decision rights, circulating observations to the programme's steering group, so that some governance visibility over the seven use cases is retained.
options.D: Accept the retrospective review as directed, but require the programme to produce system cards for all seven use cases so the eventual review has material to work with.

items.question: An Estonian online gaming company ran a shadow AI discovery exercise last year: four weeks of analysis across finance, identity and network data, producing thirty-one findings, all since registered or retired. The company already requires AI registration at project inception and at supplier onboarding. A spot check now finds twelve new unregistered uses — six browser-based tools adopted by individuals and six developer API keys — every one of which bypassed both registration points. The security lead proposes repeating the four-week exercise annually. What is the better design?

options.A: Repeat the exercise every six months rather than annually, halving the window in which new unregistered use can accumulate before anyone looks.
options.B: Turn the discovery queries into scheduled jobs that run continuously and raise a case whenever a new AI signal appears that does not reconcile to the register.
options.C: Strengthen registration at project inception and supplier onboarding, so that new use is caught as it is created rather than found months afterwards.
options.D: Target the next exercise at the business units that produced most of last year's findings, since unregistered use tends to concentrate where it was previously found.

items.question: For governance purposes, how should an AI pilot that serves real users be treated?

options.A: As an experiment running on historical or synthetic data, distinguishable from production by the fact that no live decision anywhere depends on what it produces.
options.B: As a time-boxed activity with a go or no-go decision at its end, which is what separates it from a deployment that simply runs until somebody decides to stop it.
options.C: As affecting real people and therefore requiring the same controls as production, scoped to a smaller population; the label does not reduce the obligations.
options.D: As exempt from registration until it is proposed for production, at which point it enters the inventory with its pilot results attached.

items.question: A Bangladeshi garment exporter's AI register currently holds system name, accountable owner, business unit, model and go-live date. Three downstream processes need to run from it: the annual assurance plan, which selects what to test; the incident triage desk, which sets response urgency; and the board coverage report. None of the three can currently be produced from the register. Which TWO fields should be added? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The risk tier, derived from the severity of the consequence if the output is wrong and whether output is acted on without human review.
options.B: A free-text description of the model's known limitations, copied from the provider's published documentation for that model.
options.C: The classes of data the system processes and the source systems those classes come from.
options.D: The name of the engineer who most recently changed the system's prompts or its runtime configuration.
options.E: The projected annual cost of running the system, so that the register also supports technology budget planning.

items.question: Internal audit at a Latvian digital identity provider finds that a high-tier AI use case — automated identity document verification — went live under a risk acceptance signed by a delivery manager. The firm's delegation framework places acceptance of high-tier AI risk with the executive risk committee. The system has been live for seven months and has processed 1.2 million verifications with no identified harm. What should the head of internal audit do next?

options.A: Recommend that the delegation framework be revised so delivery managers may accept high-tier AI risk where the executive risk committee cannot be convened in time.
options.B: Report the finding in the next scheduled audit report, given that the system operates normally and no harm has been identified across seven months of use.
options.C: Require the system to be withdrawn from service immediately, since it has run for seven months without a valid risk acceptance under the framework.
options.D: Escalate to the executive risk committee now so the body with authority decides on current evidence, and record the invalid acceptance as a control finding in its own right.

items.question: An Icelandic pension fund's internal audit team has started using a Claude assistant to read AI system documentation and draft audit findings. The audit committee asks the chief audit executive whether this compromises the function's independence or the reliability of its opinions. What is the correct position?

options.A: Audit's use is a registered use case like any other, the auditor remains accountable for every finding issued, and the assistant itself must be reviewed by someone outside audit.
options.B: Internal audit should not use AI to produce findings at all, because a finding produced with machine assistance cannot be defended as the auditor's own independent professional judgement.
options.C: The use needs no registration, because internal audit is an independent function whose tools are governed by its own methodology and quality standards rather than by the group AI policy.
options.D: The use is acceptable provided each report states which findings were AI-assisted, so that the audit committee can weigh those findings differently from the ones produced unaided.

items.question: In a fixed-size chunker, raising overlap from 0% to 25% has what primary effect on a production vector index?

options.A: Each chunk's embedding becomes more informative, because the 25% carried forward lengthens every window and fills more of the embedding model's input.
options.B: The store content-hashes each span at upsert and collapses the duplicated text, so vector count stays flat and answers are no longer cut at a boundary.
options.C: The vector count and storage grow, and top-k more often contains near-identical neighbouring text, in exchange for less risk of splitting an answer at a boundary.
options.D: Recall is unchanged but query latency improves, because overlapping vectors cluster tightly and the approximate search converges on a neighbourhood in fewer hops.

items.question: An aerospace MRO provider indexes 90,000 pages of maintenance manuals for its line technicians. Queries mix exact part numbers with symptom phrasing. Retrieval reliably lands on the right procedure — SMEs confirm the matched 1,200-token chunk is the correct one in 94% of sampled queries — but the generated answers routinely omit the mandatory safety warnings and prerequisite steps that appear earlier in the same procedure. The end-to-end budget is 3 seconds. What is the most effective change?

options.A: Re-chunk to roughly 250 tokens to sharpen the embedding match, and at fetch time return the whole parent procedure section that each matched chunk belongs to.
options.B: Raise chunk size to 4,000 tokens so that an entire procedure, including its warnings, prerequisites, and closing checks, fits inside one single retrievable chunk.
options.C: Raise top-k from 5 to 30 and let the model select the relevant material from the larger candidate set.
options.D: Add a cross-encoder reranker over the existing 1,200-token chunks so the best chunk is always ranked first.

items.question: At a semiconductor fab, process engineers query an equipment-knowledge assistant with strings like "EQP-4471 recurring E-0x5F2 after chamber clean". Dense-only retrieval frequently returns documents about the right kind of fault on the wrong tool. The team proposes adding a BM25 branch and fusing the two result lists. Which TWO statements correctly justify that decision? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: BM25 weights terms by corpus rarity, so a query carrying an identifier that appears in few documents ranks those documents highly, which the embedding model cannot do.
options.B: A sparse branch removes the need to embed newly ingested documents, because lexical indexes support incremental update while dense indexes require a periodic full rebuild.
options.C: BM25 is a learned sparse retriever, so it will progressively adapt to the fab's vocabulary as engineers issue more queries against it.
options.D: Dense encoders split rare identifiers into subword fragments swamped by the surrounding common words, so “EQP-4471” and “EQP-4417” land close together in vector space.
options.E: Adding a sparse branch guarantees that recall@k cannot fall for any query, because fusion only ever adds candidates to the result set.

items.question: A telco's agent-assist tool has a 700 ms p95 budget for the whole retrieval stage before generation may begin. It currently retrieves the top 50 dense candidates and reranks all 50 with a cross-encoder; the rerank step alone measures 620 ms at p95. An offline sweep shows nDCG@5 at rerank depth 20 is within 0.004 of depth 50. What should the architect do?

options.A: Keep depth 50 and batch rerank requests across concurrent users into single model calls to bring p95 down.
options.B: Drop the reranker and pass the top 15 dense hits straight to the model, relying on its long-context attention to disregard the irrelevant ones.
options.C: Cut rerank depth to 20 and spend part of the reclaimed budget on a BM25 branch fused with the dense candidates before reranking.
options.D: Keep depth 50 but start generation from the unranked candidates while the reranker runs, amending the streamed answer if the final ordering differs.

items.question: Why can a cross-encoder reranker not replace the vector index as the first-stage retriever over a ten-million-passage corpus?

options.A: It scores each query–passage pair jointly at inference time, so ranking the corpus would require one forward pass per passage per query.
options.B: It emits only a binary relevant/not-relevant label, which provides no ordering to rank by.
options.C: It requires the entire corpus to be re-scored whenever a single document is added or changed.
options.D: It truncates any input longer than a single sentence, so most passages in a realistic corpus could not be scored at all without first being split into fragments.

items.question: A national tax authority runs an internal guidance assistant for its 6,000 caseworkers. The retrieval dashboard reports context precision@5 of 0.91 and the reranker has been carefully tuned. Nevertheless, subject-matter reviewers judge 22% of answers materially incorrect. Reading through a sample of the failures, an engineer notices that in most of them the passage containing the governing rule does not appear anywhere in the five retrieved chunks. What is the best next step?

options.A: Move the generator to a higher capability tier, since the current model is evidently failing to reason correctly over the guidance material it is being given.
options.B: Replace the reranker with a stronger cross-encoder so that the governing rule is promoted above the near-miss passages.
options.C: Raise top-k from 5 to 25 and re-measure end-to-end answer accuracy against the reviewer judgements.
options.D: Measure context recall against the reviewer-annotated gold passages, at k=5 and at a much larger candidate depth, before changing any retrieval parameter.

items.question: An HR-technology SaaS serves 3,400 employer tenants from one platform. The largest tenant holds 900,000 documents, the smallest holds 40. The company is SOC 2 audited and a cross-tenant disclosure is a contract-terminating event. The engineering team proposes a single shared vector index with a `tenant_id` metadata filter on every query. What is the defensible architectural position?

options.A: Post-filtering the ANN results by `tenant_id` is equivalent in safety and avoids the recall penalty that pre-filtering imposes on large indexes.
options.B: A shared index with filtering is acceptable if the filter is a server-side pre-filter derived from the authenticated session, with an automated cross-tenant probe on every deploy.
options.C: Metadata filtering can never provide tenant isolation; each of the 3,400 tenants requires a physically separate index.
options.D: Isolation can be enforced in the prompt by supplying each chunk's `tenant_id` alongside its text and instructing Claude to disregard any chunk whose tenant does not match the requesting user.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company indexes 60,000 clinical study reports, each producing roughly 400 chunks. Medical writers find that retrieved chunks are unusable in isolation — a chunk reading "the primary endpoint was met at week 24" does not say which study, which arm, or which endpoint. The team wants to adopt contextual retrieval, generating a short situating preamble for every chunk with an LLM before embedding it. The platform lead objects that 24 million generation calls is not affordable. Which plan best addresses the objection while preserving the technique's benefit?

options.A: Move the augmentation to query time: retrieve the top-k chunks first, then have a model write a situating preamble for each before passing them to the generator.
options.B: Abandon augmentation and rerank the top 100 dense candidates with a cross-encoder that reads each chunk jointly with the query to settle which study it belongs to.
options.C: Process one report at a time with the whole report in a cached prompt prefix reused across its chunk-context calls, and submit the ingest job through the Batch API.
options.D: Generate the preamble from the chunk itself plus the report title and identifier using the cheapest model tier, avoiding any need to read the surrounding document.

items.question: A public-sector benefits agency refreshes its guidance index nightly. The job re-parses any document whose source-system hash changed and upserts the resulting chunks by deterministic chunk id. Caseworkers report that guidance formally withdrawn three months ago is still being cited in answers, and that superseded paragraphs from documents that were shortened still appear. What is the root cause and the correct fix?

options.A: Upsert-only refresh never deletes; the job must reconcile each document's chunk-id set and delete the orphans, and withdrawal must raise an explicit delete.
options.B: Approximate nearest-neighbour graphs cannot process deletions at all, so the index must be rebuilt from scratch each night to reflect withdrawals and shortened documents.
options.C: Add an exponential decay on each chunk's last-published date to the ranking score, so current guidance consistently outranks withdrawn and superseded material.
options.D: Attach a `status` field to each chunk and render it as a header line above the passage, instructing the model to ignore anything marked withdrawn or superseded.

items.question: Which attribute is best carried as filterable chunk metadata rather than concatenated into the text that is embedded?

options.A: The heading of the section the chunk sits under.
options.B: The name of the product that the chunk describes, which users routinely mention by name when they type their queries into the assistant's search box.
options.C: A one-sentence summary of the parent document.
options.D: The date range over which the document was in force, used to restrict answers to the guidance applicable on a stated date.

items.question: A broadcast media archive holds 40 million indexed chunks and wants to move to a newer embedding model with a different output dimensionality. Measured throughput means a full re-embed of the corpus takes about eleven days. Editorial search must remain available throughout, and the newsroom will not accept a period of visibly degraded results. Which migration plan is correct?

options.A: Re-embed in place with a rolling job that overwrites each vector by chunk id, so the live index converges to the new model over eleven days with no second copy.
options.B: Build a second index with the new model in parallel, dual-write new content to both, and cut over behind a flag once it matches the live index on the retrieval eval set.
options.C: Apply a random projection to the new model's output so it matches the existing dimensionality, allowing new vectors to be written into the current index with no reindex.
options.D: Keep both models' vectors in the live index, query the old and new fields together, and blend the two similarity scores so quality improves as coverage grows.

items.question: An energy utility's field-operations assistant is used in multi-turn sessions. Technicians open with a specific asset — "pull up the inspection history for transformer T-118 at Ashby substation" — and then ask short follow-ups such as "what's the torque spec for that flange?". The follow-up turns retrieve poorly because the embedded query carries no referent. Which TWO changes address the cause? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Rewrite each user turn into a standalone, self-contained query using the conversation history, and perform retrieval on the rewritten form rather than the raw turn.
options.B: Embed the concatenation of the entire conversation so far, guaranteeing that the referent is always present somewhere inside the query vector however the follow-up turn happens to be phrased.
options.C: Perform the rewrite inside the same model call that generates the answer, so the additional step adds no latency to the turn.
options.D: Carry entities resolved earlier in the session — asset id, site — forward as retrieval filters, so the search stays scoped even when the phrasing is vague.
options.E: Raise top-k for follow-up turns specifically, so the correct passage has more opportunity to appear in the candidate set.

items.question: A mid-size insurer is building a policy-wording assistant over 2.3 million chunks. The authoritative policy, endorsement, and state-filing tables already live in a well-run PostgreSQL cluster. Nearly every query filters on line of business, state, and effective date, and the business requires that a retrieved chunk and the structured policy record it belongs to never disagree. The platform team is four engineers. The team lead proposes adopting a dedicated vector database "because that is what everyone uses". What should the architect recommend?

options.A: Load the vectors from object storage into application memory at startup and brute-force similarity in-process, removing the database from the retrieval path entirely.
options.B: Adopt the dedicated vector database, since approximate nearest-neighbour recall at 2.3 million vectors is unacceptable in a relational engine whatever index type is used.
options.C: Use a vector extension in the existing PostgreSQL cluster: ANN is adequate at this size, filters join the authoritative tables, and there is no second store to run.
options.D: Store the vectors in PostgreSQL and replicate every chunk into a dedicated vector store as well, so either system can serve traffic and the team can migrate later without pressure.
